sections.label: THE PROBLEM
sections.heading: Have we lost touch with nature?

lines: Around 56% of the world's population lives in cities; the UN projects roughly 68% by 2050.
People spend most of their day (an estimated ~90%) indoors.
'The attention economy': screens and notifications keep the mind constantly stimulated.
The result: chronic stress, attention fatigue and a systematic drift away from nature.

items.def: Most of the population is urban, and rising

sections.source: Source: UN World Urbanization Prospects; EPA indoor-air studies

items.text: Japanese for 'forest bath'. It means immersing yourself — not in water, but in the forest's atmosphere, light, sound and scent — with all five senses, slowly and without purpose. It is not physical exercise but a practice of sensory presence.

lines: The term was coined in 1982 by Japan's Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (Tomohide Akiyama).
Aim: to encourage the public to connect with forests and to raise the value of forest areas.
From the 1990s, Yoshifumi Miyazaki and his team carried out the first physiological measurements.
Over time it grew into an interdisciplinary research field called 'forest medicine'.

items.def: The year the concept was born

items.text: Japan · public health and forest policy

lines: It comes from the Latin root 'silva' (forest); it refers to the therapeutic contact established with trees and the forest environment.
Shinrin-yoku is an experiential practice of Japanese origin; silvotherapy is a broader, cross-cultural umbrella term.
In this training the two complement each other: the scientific-experiential backbone comes from shinrin-yoku.
The therapeutic intent and framework, meanwhile, draw on the silvotherapy tradition.

sections.label: THEORETICAL FOUNDATION
sections.heading: Biophilia: why does nature do us good?

lines: Biologist E.O. Wilson (1984): because humans spent almost all of their evolution in nature, we carry an innate affinity for living things.
'The savannah hypothesis': open, wooded, water-rich landscapes are preferred across many cultures and found calming.
Stephen Kellert carried this into architecture as 'biophilic design'.
Biophilia is not proof; it is an explanatory framework that makes sense of the 'why' behind the physiological findings.

items.def: A framework; not a hard law

sections.label: SCIENTIFIC MEASUREMENT
sections.heading: We can measure connection to nature

lines: Connection to nature is now a measurable psychological construct: 'Nature Relatedness' (Nisbet) and the 'Connectedness to Nature Scale' (Mayer & Frantz).
Research links a strong connection to nature with better mental health, positive affect and life satisfaction.
Forest bathing aims not merely at 'being there' but at deepening this connection.
The guide's job is to help participants strengthen their own relationship with nature.

sections.label: THE OPPORTUNITY
sections.heading: A fertile ground: the global opportunity

lines: Forests cover roughly 31% of the world's land area (FAO) — an enormous diversity of ecosystems, from coast to mountain.
Urban forests, national parks and nature reserves offer accessible session venues.
Rising urban stress and burnout are increasing demand for complementary approaches.
In many regions, structured training and service provision remain limited despite clear demand — this is an opportunity.

sections.source: Source: FAO, Global Forest Resources Assessment

sections.label: ROLE
sections.heading: What the guide does and does not do

lines: Does: sets a safe framework, holds the rhythm, opens the senses through invitations, creates a non-judgemental space.
Does: helps participants build their own relationship with nature.
Does not: lecture, 'explain' nature, manage the experience, or diagnose.
Does not: practise psychotherapy or give medical advice.

items.def: It is not a clinical role

items.text: This training makes you a guide who SUPPORTS psychological wellbeing through forest bathing. It does NOT grant authority in clinical psychology, psychotherapy or medical treatment. The guide works in a complementary way with stress, anxiety and burnout, does not diagnose, and refers to a mental-health professional when needed.
This boundary will be repeated throughout the programme.

sections.label: SCOPE
sections.heading: For whom and within what scope?

lines: Target audience: wellness/life coaches, nature and outdoor guides, yoga/meditation instructors, and enthusiasts.
For mental-health practitioners: adding a nature-based, complementary method to their practice.
No prerequisites; an interest in nature and people, plus access to an accessible green space, is enough.
Scope: non-clinical, complementary wellbeing guidance.

items.text: 'The three-breath threshold': take three slow breaths in front of the window/camera and count only the sounds you can hear (live, 5 min).

items.def: Homework: 15 minutes of phone-free, goalless presence in a nearby green space; then a one-paragraph reflection note.
Self-assess: apply a few items from a nature-connection scale (NR/CNS) to yourself and reflect.
Reflection: 'When did I last spend time in nature with no purpose at all?'

lines: Forest bathing = slow, sensory, purposeless presence; not a walk or exercise.
The concept was born in 1982 and is today a peer-reviewed research field.
Biophilia and nature-connection scales provide the theoretical and measurable foundation.
The guide is complementary; they do not provide clinical treatment.

items.text: The volatile organic compounds that trees release into the air to protect themselves from insects, fungi and bacteria (alpha-pinene, beta-pinene, limonene, camphene…). They are the source of the forest's characteristic scent and, when inhaled, can influence human immunity.

sections.label: IMMUNITY
sections.heading: Phytoncides and NK cells (Li)

lines: Qing Li and his team (2007): 12 male participants, a 3-day forest trip.
In 11 of 12 participants, NK ('natural killer') cell activity increased by ~50%.
NK cell counts and anti-cancer proteins (perforin, granulysin, granzyme A/B) rose.
Alpha- and beta-pinene were detected in forest air; in city air they were almost absent.

sections.source: Source: Li Q. et al. (2007), Int. J. Immunopathol. Pharmacol.

sections.label: PERSISTENCE & CONTROL
sections.heading: How long does the effect last?

lines: The elevated NK activity remained high for at least 7 days after the trip.
In the same team's city-trip study, NO increase in NK activity was seen — the effect is specific to the forest.
A study with female participants produced similar results.
Practical takeaway: regular (e.g. monthly) forest contact may help sustain the effect.

sections.label: STRESS BIOMARKERS
sections.heading: Park 2010: a field experiment across 24 forests

lines: Park, Tsunetsugu, Miyazaki et al.: crossover-design field experiments in 24 different forests across Japan.
Participants walked and viewed the scenery for 20 minutes each in forest and urban settings.
Compared with the city, the forest environment: lower cortisol, heart rate and blood pressure.
Also, higher parasympathetic and lower sympathetic nervous activity.

sections.source: Source: Park B.J. et al. (2010), Environ. Health Prev. Med. 15:18–26

sections.label: STRENGTH OF EVIDENCE
sections.heading: Cortisol: what does the meta-analysis say?

lines: Antonelli et al. (2019): a systematic review of 22 studies, a meta-analysis of 8 studies.
In forest groups, salivary cortisol was significantly lower than in urban groups.
The effect is short-term and real; expectation/placebo may also contribute.
Combining multiple studies provides stronger evidence than any single study.

sections.source: Source: Antonelli M. et al. (2019), Int. J. Biometeorol. 63:1117–1134

lines: Natural scenes are evolutionarily 'safe'
The stress response drops quickly and largely unconsciously

lines: Phytoncides (via smell) → effects on immunity and stress hormones.
Natural sound and visual scenery → calming of the autonomic nervous system (SRT).
Effortless attention → restoration of attention capacity (ART).
All together: lower stress, better mood, renewed focus.

items.text: Most studies have relatively small samples and are short-term; effects vary by forest, season, duration and individual. The right message: forest bathing has consistent and promising positive effects on stress, mood and physiology — but this is not a cure for illness; it is a health-supporting complementary practice.
Correlation is not causation; exaggeration undermines trust.
Group rehearsal: an ethically and scientifically balanced response to a client who says 'forest bathing cures cancer'.

items.def: Homework: in one session, observe each of the five senses for 2 minutes each and note which sense is most calming.
Concept card: write ART and SRT in one sentence each, in your own words; add a real example.
Source reading: read the abstract of Park (2010) or Li (2007) and produce a single paragraph.

lines: Phytoncides support NK cells and anti-cancer proteins (effect 7+ days).
The forest lowers cortisol, heart rate and blood pressure; it strengthens the parasympathetic system (Park, Antonelli).
ART restores the mind, SRT eases stress — together they explain the picture.
The science is promising but not a treatment; an honest framing is essential.

sections.label: STARTING POINT
sections.heading: The modern mind: stress and attention fatigue

lines: Urban life tires the mind with constant stimuli, notifications and decision load.
This feeds both the chronic stress response and 'attention fatigue'.
Forest bathing works in two directions: physiological calming + connection to the present moment.
The goal is not to 'solve the problem' but to open space for the person's own capacity to self-regulate.

items.def: Anchors the mind to the present

sections.label: MOOD
sections.heading: POMS: how does the forest change mood?
sections.source: Source: Field studies based on the Profile of Mood States (POMS)

sections.label: CLINICAL SYMPTOMS
sections.heading: Anxiety and depressive symptoms

lines: Meta-analyses of randomised and quasi-experimental studies indicate that forest-based interventions can produce significant improvement in depression and anxiety symptoms.
On the POMS, Total Mood Disturbance (TMD) decreases and vigour increases.
Effect sizes vary; the strongest results are seen in structured, guided programmes.
A critical distinction: these are 'symptom relief' findings — not the treatment of a clinical diagnosis.

sections.source: Source: Forest-therapy and mental-health meta-analyses (including RCTs)

items.text: Turning the same negative thought over and over — 'the mind stuck on the same track'. It is one of the strongest cognitive risk factors for depression and anxiety. Turning towards nature moves attention outward, out of this internal loop, and naturally interrupts rumination.

sections.label: BRAIN EVIDENCE
sections.heading: Bratman 2015: breaking the loop

lines: 38 participants were randomly assigned to a 90-minute walk in either a natural or an urban setting (Stanford).
The nature walk reduced both self-reported rumination and activity in the subgenual prefrontal cortex (sgPFC).
The sgPFC is a region associated with negative self-focused thought.
These effects were NOT seen on the urban walk — the difference is specific to nature.

sections.source: Source: Bratman G.N. et al. (2015), PNAS 112(28):8567–8572

lines: At its core, forest bathing is a mindfulness practice built on non-judgemental observation and returning to the present moment.
The difference: the 'object of attention' is nature itself, and it holds attention easily, without forcing it.
Mindfulness's proven basis in stress, anxiety and depression strengthens this practice.
For participants with mindfulness experience, this bridge is very natural.
Nature acts as a safe 'holding environment': a person can make contact with their emotions without suppressing them.
Trees, seasons and cycles strengthen a sense of perspective, belonging and meaning.
This opens space for self-compassion — treating yourself as kindly as you would a friend.
The guide gently invites this dimension through appropriate invitations, never forcing it: 'a tree grows without judging itself.'

sections.label: SAFETY
sections.heading: Red flags: when to stop and refer?

items.def: Attending under the influence of alcohol/substances

items.text: A forest bathing guide is NOT a psychotherapist. When a red flag appears, the guide stops safely and without judgement, prioritises the person's safety, and refers them to a mental-health professional or an emergency line. The guide's strength lies in knowing their limits; an 'I can fix everything' attitude puts both the participant and the guide at risk.
Have local crisis and support lines ready in advance.
Role-play: rehearse a non-judgemental, boundary-keeping response to a participant who starts crying during a session.

items.def: Homework: after 20 minutes in nature, rate your 'pre/post rumination' state of mind on a scale of 1–10.
Red-flag list: write the referral criteria for your own target group.
Reflection: 'In which situations should I refer a participant to a professional?'

lines: The forest reduces rumination and sgPFC activity (Bratman); it improves mood (POMS).
Forest bathing = nature-based mindfulness + emotion regulation + meaning.
The effects are symptom relief; they do not replace clinical treatment.
At a red flag, the guide stops and refers safely.

items.def: A summary of the anatomy of a session

items.text: 'The forest is the therapist; the guide merely opens the door.' The guide is not an expert-authority but a humble intermediary who facilitates the relationship between the participant and nature. They do not lecture, do not 'explain' nature, do not manage the experience — they set a safe framework, hold the rhythm and open space for the participant's own discovery.
Without this attitude, the techniques ring hollow.

lines: Humility: not an expert but a facilitator; the experience belongs to the participant.
Trust: setting a safe, predictable framework calms the nervous system.
Patience: tolerating silence and slowness; not filling the gap.
Self-regulation: the guide helps the group through their own calm (co-regulation).

lines: The Standard Sequence is a 'journey' arc: entry gate → deepening → sharing → exit gate.
A full session often lasts 2–3 hours; the aim is depth, not speed.
The skeleton is flexible: the guide adapts it to the time, the group and the terrain (Module 5).
Each stage deepens the trust opened by the one before.

sections.label: STRUCTURE
sections.heading: The three qualities of a good invitation

lines: Open-ended: there is no 'right answer'; the participant turns towards their own experience.
Sensory: it calls on the body and the senses, not mental analysis.
Timeless/non-judgemental: it doesn't rush, it sets no expectation of success.
Collaboration with nature: a steep path invites slowing down, clouds invite looking, a bird invites spreading your wings.

items.def: Contact with the ground, the rhythm of the breath

items.text: First the near sounds, then the far ones
The warmth of the air, the scents

items.def: Long silences are left between each sense. The aim is not to 'achieve' something but to slow the nervous system.

sections.label: MASTERY
sections.heading: Pace, silence and the guide's body

lines: The most common mistake of a novice guide: rushing and filling the gaps with talk.
Silence is a tool: after giving the invitation, fall silent and allow time (at least a few minutes).
The guide's body is also a message: slow movement, relaxed shoulders, a calm and low tone of voice.
This says 'it's safe here, you can slow down'; the group regulates through the guide's calm.

sections.label: THE GOLDEN RULE
sections.heading: Offer the invitation, then step back

items.text: After offering an invitation, the most powerful move is to do nothing. Stop talking, return to your own presence, and open up real time for the participant to live their experience. The art of guiding is as much about when you fall silent as about what you say.
Silence is not a gap to be filled but the experience itself.
Live: the trainer guides the 'Pleasures of Presence' invitation in real time for 10 minutes; participants experience it.

items.def: Homework: each participant writes an original 3-minute 'invitation' and records it aloud.
In pairs: offer each other a short invitation and give constructive feedback.
Self-review: listen to your own recording and assess it for pace and silence.

lines: The forest is the therapist; the guide opens the door (a humble, facilitating role).
The Standard Sequence is a safe, flexible, seven-stage skeleton.
An invitation is an open-ended, sensory and non-judgemental offer; not an instruction.
Silence and pace are the most powerful guiding tools.

lines: Target audience: individuals, corporate teams, wellness centres, collaboration with therapists.
Format: a single session, a series programme, a corporate event, a nature camp/retreat.
A transparent promise: what is and isn't offered; honest language — not a miracle, but an evidence-based experience.
Local channels: urban forests, national parks, municipal/corporate partnerships, hotels/retreats.
Write a one-sentence value proposition: to whom, what value and how do you offer it?
Pricing is set according to the market, duration and format; don't undervalue your work.
Differentiation: your area of specialism (e.g. burnout, corporate, family) sets you apart.
Avoid exaggerated health claims in your promotion; trust is the foundation of long-term work.

items.def: A few sentences of open-ended reflection

lines: Inform the participant and obtain their consent; participation is voluntary.
Store data confidentially; comply with data-protection law (e.g. GDPR).
Use measurement to improve the service, not for exaggerated claims.
Even a simple before/after comparison makes progress visible.

items.def: No diagnosis or treatment; not clinical

lines: A guide who holds space for others must also keep their own nervous system cared for.
A regular personal forest bathing practice, peer support and, where possible, supervision.
Don't carry the emotional load alone; after a difficult session, make time for your own regulation.
Continuous development: reading, further training, practice in different ecosystems.

sections.label: REFRAMING
sections.heading: Self-care is not a luxury but a responsibility

items.text: A burnt-out guide cannot hold a safe space. Protecting your own wellbeing is an inseparable part of the quality and ethical safety of the service you offer. Show yourself the same care you show your participants.
You too are part of the forest — open space for yourself as well.

lines: Days 0–30: do your recces, identify 2–3 places, prepare your safety plans.
Days 30–60: run 3 free/discounted trial sessions; collect feedback and measurements.
Days 60–90: clarify your value proposition, set your pricing, announce your first paid programme.
Ongoing: personal practice, peer support and a habit of record-keeping.

items.text: Final project: prepare a six-component portfolio (submitted after the course).

items.def: Value proposition: write a one-sentence proposition for your own practice.
90-day plan: write who, where and when you will run your first three trial sessions.
Closing ritual: a gratitude circle and intention sharing as a group.

lines: Build an ethical, transparent and measurable practice; stay faithful to the boundary of scope.
Track your impact with simple validated scales and improve your service.
Self-care is a professional responsibility.
Earn the 'Certificate of Completion' with the final project.

items.text: Take good care of the forest, of your participants and of yourself. May your path be clear.
